newsitem.title: ROMANIA: ROMANIA ASSESSES CROP DAMAGE FROM FLOODING, RAIN.
newsitem.headline: ROMANIA ASSESSES CROP DAMAGE FROM FLOODING, RAIN.

text.p: Heavy rainfalls in recent weeks have flooded tens of thousands of hectares of Romanian cropland and delayed sowing and seasonal work, the agriculture ministry said on Wednesday.
Ministry data showed some 89,000 hectares of farmland were under water or had recorded an "excess of humidity", compared to 18,000 ha a week ago.
Weather forecasters saw little letup in rainfall over the next week and officials said crops on the land could be lost. Rainfalls exceeding 15 litres per square metre were expected in most areas.
"For the time being, one can say that part of the crops under water can still be saved," a ministry official said.
"I'm very much afraid that these figures are only preliminary and one should expect more reports on damage in the coming days," another ministry official said.
Of the 89,000 ha affected by the bad weather, some 35,000 were under wheat, 11,800 ha sown to barley, 2,950 sown to fodder plants while 37,300 ha were unsown, the data showed.
"Those crops will be lost if bad weather continues and farmers are unable to drain the water. And things could worsen if rains don't stop and floods continue," an official said.
Central and southern Romania have been hit by a series of heavy rains and cold snaps in recent weeks.
The Environment Ministry said on Wednesday the main rivers in central Transylvania had flooded, while levels of scores of small rivers across Romania had reached emergency levels.

Reports in the local media said floods also caused by melting snow in the mountains, in some areas exceeding 2.5 metres, had submerged scores of households and disrupted road and rail traffic in central Romnania.
The ministry official complained that bad weather had forced farmers to delay sowing of maize and sugar beet, planned on 3.13 million ha and 138,400 ha respectively.

"Sowing of maize should have been completed by this time of the year," the official said. But farmers, he said, could still bring in a "good" maize crop provided they resort to seeds with a shorter period of germination.
Sowing of fodder plants had also been delayed, he said.
